_description: Material technique: Erosion effect. Progressive wear/damage revealing layers underneath. Used for destruction, aging, terrain blending, and stylized dissolve variants.
overview: Erosion is a variant of dissolve but with directional, layered, or physically-motivated progression. Instead of random noise-based disappearance, erosion simulates wear patterns — edges erode first, thin areas break before thick, and underlying layers are revealed progressively.

material_setup.blend_mode: Masked or Opaque (with World Position Offset for vertex displacement)

ErosionDirection.note: Optional: direction of erosion progression (e.g., bottom-up, inside-out)

ErosionDetailScale.note: Fine grain detail noise layered on top

steps.note: Use Perlin or Worley/Voronoi noise for natural wear patterns

steps.nodes: Second noise at ErosionDetailScale, multiply with base noise (0.3 weight)
steps.note: Creates micro-detail crumbling at erosion edges

steps.nodes: Dot(VertexNormalWS, ErosionDirection) → remap 0-1 → blend with noise mask
steps.note: Makes erosion start from a direction (e.g., wind-facing side erodes first)

steps.nodes: Use AmbientOcclusion or curvature map to make edges/thin parts erode faster
steps.note: Multiply AO into erosion mask — dark AO areas (crevices, edges) erode first
Same principle as dissolve but with richer input mask
Can use this for: emissive glow, color shift, or reveal underlayer
e.g., metal surface erodes to reveal rust, wood reveals charcoal, stone reveals magma

frost_erosion.direction: typically bottom-up or from contact point

age_wear.noise_type: Perlin + AO-biased (edges and corners wear first)

performance_notes.texture_reads: 2-3 noise samples is acceptable. Avoid >4 for mobile/VR.
performance_notes.optimization: Can bake direction + curvature + noise into single RGBA texture to reduce samples

common_mistakes: Using only one noise frequency → erosion looks too uniform and CG
Erosion edges too sharp without any softness → looks like z-fighting, not wear
Not revealing underlying layer → just disappears, misses storytelling opportunity
Direction uniform across whole mesh → real erosion varies by exposure/geometry
Forgetting to add slight vertex displacement at edge → eroded surface looks 2D flat
